title: 22. Interview: MongoDB
summary: Interview Q&A for MongoDB — 14 questions with model answers.
objectives: Answer 14 MongoDB interview questions out loud
Lead with the concept, then a small example, then a tradeoff

sections.title: Conceptual Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. What is the difference between a MongoDB document and a relational row?
**Answer:** A relational **row** is a flat tuple conforming to a fixed schema — every row in a table has the same columns, types, and constraints; if you add a column, you must run `ALTER TABLE` for all existing rows. A MongoDB **document** is a nested, JSON-like object (stored as BSON) with no enforced schema — different documents in the same collection can have totally different fields. Documents can contain arrays and sub-documents natively (`{ address: { city: "NYC", geo: [40.7, -74.0] } }`), modeling aggregates that would require multiple tables and joins in SQL. The trade-off: relational rows give you **schema enforcement** at the DB layer (constraints, foreign keys, types), which protects data integrity; documents give you **schema flexibility**, which speeds up development but allows "schema drift" — different teams inserting subtly different shapes. In practice, applications still define an application-level schema (via Mongoose, Pydantic, etc.); the DB is just lenient about enforcement. Real-world: a CMS that stores laptop and shirt products in one collection is natural in MongoDB but awkward in SQL.
**Visual:**
```
Relational row (flat, fixed schema):
  users(id, name, email, created_at)
  -> (1, "alice", "a@x.com", 2024-01-01)

MongoDB document (nested, flexible):
  users collection:
  { _id: 1, name: "alice", contacts: { email: "a@x.com",
                                       phone: "+1-555" },
    prefs: { theme: "dark", lang: "en" } }

Schema enforcement: SQL=database, MongoDB=application layer.
```

### Q2. How does a MongoDB replica set handle failover?
**Answer:** A replica set has one **primary** (accepts writes) and N **secondaries** (replicate the primary's oplog). Each node sends heartbeats to peers every 2 seconds; if a secondary doesn't hear from the primary within the election timeout (default 10 seconds), it calls for an election. Elections use a Raft-derived protocol: each candidate requests votes from peers, and the node with the most up-to-date oplog wins a majority vote (this prevents a stale secondary from becoming primary). Election typically completes in 10-30 seconds. The MongoDB driver maintains connections to all replica-set members and tracks which is primary; on failover, it automatically reconnects to the new primary — no application code change needed. **Caveat**: writes that the old primary acknowledged with `w:1` but didn't yet replicate to a majority are **rolled back** when that primary recovers (the rollback data is written to a `rollback` collection for inspection). To eliminate rollback risk, use `w:majority` write concern — the primary won't ack until the write is replicated to a majority, guaranteeing it survives any single-node failure. Trade-off: `w:majority` adds ~5-15 ms of replication latency per write.
**Visual:**
```
T=0   Primary P, Secondaries S1, S2.  P accepts write w1 (w:1 ack)
T=1   P streams oplog(w1) -> S1 (not yet S2)
T=2   P dies (network partition / host crash)
T=3   S1, S2 miss 3 heartbeats -> election called
T=12  S2 elected primary (it has the same oplog as S1 in this case)
T=13  Driver reconnects to S2
T=14  P recovers, rejoins as secondary. w1 NOT in S2's oplog -> ROLLBACK
      (w1 written to P's rollback/ dir for manual recovery)

With w:majority: P wouldn't have acked w1 until S1+S2 had it.
                -> w1 survives, no rollback.
```

### Q3. What is the role of the mongos router and config servers in a sharded cluster?
**Answer:** In a sharded cluster, **mongos** is the stateless query router — clients connect to `mongos` (never directly to shards), and `mongos` decides which shard(s) to forward each operation to. **Config servers** are a 3-node replica set storing cluster metadata: the list of shards, databases, collections, and the **chunk-to-shard mapping** (which shard owns which range of shard-key values). When `mongos` receives a query with the shard key, it consults the cached chunk map and routes directly to the owning shard — single-hop, fast. When the query lacks a shard key, `mongos` does a **scatter-gather** — fans out to all shards and merges the results, which is much slower (latency = slowest shard). The **balancer** runs on the config-server primary and periodically checks chunk sizes; if a shard has too many chunks, it migrates chunks to underloaded shards (during low-traffic windows by default). Config servers are critical: if all three die, the cluster can't route queries — which is why they're a 3-node replica set with `w:majority`. Real-world: a 100-shard cluster might have 5-10 `mongos` instances behind a load balancer for HA and throughput.
**Visual:**
```
              +---------+
              | client  |
              +----+----+
                   |
              +----v----+
              | mongos  | (stateless, horizontally scalable)
              +----+----+
                   |
        +----------+----------+
        |  consult config     |
        v                     v
+----------------+    +----------------+
| config servers |    | shards (RS)    |
| (3-node RS)    |    | 1, 2, ..., N   |
| chunk -> shard |    +----------------+
+----------------+
```

### Q4. Why is shard-key choice in MongoDB described as "the most important decision you'll make"?
**Answer:** The shard key determines (1) which shard owns each document, (2) which queries can be routed to a single shard vs. scatter-gathered, and (3) write-hotspot risk. Three cardinal sins: **(a) Monotonic shard key** (like `ObjectId` or `timestamp`) — all new documents fall into the highest range, so all writes funnel to a single "hot" shard, defeating the point of sharding. Fix: use a **hashed shard key** (`{ _id: "hashed" }`) to spread writes evenly, but you lose range queries on `_id`. **(b) Low-cardinality shard key** (like `country` with 10 values) — you can never have more than 10 chunks, so you can't scale beyond 10 shards. Fix: compound with a high-cardinality field (`{ country: 1, user_id: 1 }`). **(c) Shard key absent from common queries** — if you shard by `user_id` but most queries filter by `tenant_id`, every query scatter-gathers. Fix: shard by the field most queries filter on. Shard keys are **essentially immutable** before MongoDB 4.4 (you'd have to dump and reload the collection); 4.4+ allows `refineCollectionShardKey` (adding suffix fields) and 5.0+ allows `reshardCollection` (full key change, but it's an expensive online operation that doubles disk usage). Real-world: eBay initially sharded by `itemId` (ObjectId), hit write hotspots during big sales, and migrated to `{ categoryId: 1, itemId: 1 }`.
**Visual:**
```
Shard-key cardinal sins:

  Bad #1: monotonic (_id = ObjectId)
    chunk1: [..., oid_1000]   chunk2: [oid_1001, oid_2000]   chunk3: [oid_2001, ...]
    ALL new inserts hit chunk3 -> hot shard, no write scaling.

  Bad #2: low cardinality (country=US/EU/APAC)
    Max 3 chunks -> max 3 shards -> hard ceiling.

  Bad #3: queries don't use shard key
    shard by user_id, query by tenant_id -> scatter-gather (slow).

  Good: { tenant_id: 1, created_at: 1 } (compound)
    + high cardinality (many tenants)
    + writes spread across tenants
    + tenant-scoped range queries route to one shard
    + time-ordered within tenant (range queries work)
```

### Q5. What is the aggregation pipeline and how does the optimizer transform it?
**Answer:** The aggregation pipeline is a chain of stages (`$match`, `$group`, `$sort`, `$project`, `$lookup`, `$unwind`, `$facet`, etc.) that transforms documents — MongoDB's equivalent of SQL's `SELECT...GROUP BY...JOIN`. Each stage takes a stream of documents and emits a stream; the engine executes them in order, but the **optimizer** reorders and merges stages for efficiency. Key optimizations: **(1) `$match` pushdown** — `$match` is moved as early as possible so it can use indexes and reduce the working set before later stages. **(2) `$project` pushdown** — projected-away fields are dropped early to shrink documents in the pipeline. **(3) `$sort` + `$limit` merge** — `$sort` followed by `$limit` becomes a top-K heap sort instead of a full sort (huge memory savings). **(4) `$lookup` optimization** — if the foreign collection has an index on the join field, `$lookup` uses it instead of scanning. **(5) `$group` uses indexes** when the group key is indexed. The pipeline can also be split across shards in a sharded cluster: each shard runs the prefix locally, then `mongos` merges the partial results. Real-world: a `orders` → `$match` (last 30 days) → `$lookup` (users) → `$group` (by user) → `$sort` (by revenue) → `$limit` (top 100) pipeline processes millions of orders in seconds thanks to these optimizations.
**Visual:**
```
Written pipeline:
  $match (region=US) -> $project (drop internal fields)
  -> $group (sum revenue by customer) -> $sort (revenue desc)
  -> $limit 100

Optimizer transforms to:
  $match (region=US) [uses index on region]
  + $project fused (drops fields early at scan time)
  -> $group (partial per shard if sharded)
  -> $sort + $limit fused = top-K heap (memory: O(K), not O(N))
  -> merge at mongos (if sharded)

Result: 10x-100x faster than naive sequential execution.
```

### Q6. What does WiredTiger do better than the old MMAPv1 storage engine?
**Answer:** **MMAPv1** (MongoDB's original engine, deprecated in 4.0) used memory-mapped files with **collection-level locking** — only one writer per collection at a time, which made write throughput collapse under concurrency. It also didn't compress data on disk, and updates that grew a document forced expensive relocation. **WiredTiger** (default since 3.2) fixes all three: **(1) Document-level locking** — two writers updating different documents in the same collection run concurrently, so write throughput scales with concurrency (typically 7-10× higher than MMAPv1). **(2) Snappy compression by default** — documents and indexes are compressed ~50-70%, halving disk usage and RAM footprint (more of the working set fits in cache). **(3) MVCC** — readers see a consistent snapshot, writers create new versions, so readers and writers never block each other (similar to PostgreSQL's MVCC). WiredTiger also supports **Zlib** (better compression, slower) and **Zstd** (best of both, since 4.2). It uses **B-tree indexes** (vs. MMAPv1's B-tree but without prefix compression) and a **write-ahead log** fsync'd per write concern for crash recovery. The trade-off: WiredTiger uses more RAM for its cache (default `--wiredTigerCacheSizeGB` is 50% of system RAM) and has slightly higher per-write CPU cost — but the throughput gain is worth it. Real-world: Adobe's migration from MMAPv1 to WiredTiger cut their storage footprint by ~60% and tripled write throughput.
**Visual:**
```
                    MMAPv1                  WiredTiger
                    -------                 ----------
Locking             collection-level        document-level
                    (1 writer/collection)   (many writers/collection)
Concurrency         P + P block             P + P parallel
                    W + W block             W + W parallel (diff docs)
Compression         none                    Snappy (default)
Storage footprint   1.0x                    ~0.4x
Crash recovery      journal (optional)      WAL (mandatory)
MVCC                no                      yes (snapshot reads)
Write throughput    1x baseline             7-10x baseline
Status              removed in 4.2          default since 3.2
```

### Q7. What is the difference between read concern, write concern, and read preference?
**Answer:** These are three independent dials controlling consistency, durability, and routing in MongoDB. **Write concern** (`w:`) governs *durability* of writes — `w:0` fire-and-forget, `w:1` primary ack, `w:majority` majority-of-replica-set ack (survives failover), plus optional `j:true` to fsync the journal. Higher = more durable but slower. **Read concern** governs *freshness* of reads — `local` reads the primary's latest in-memory state (may roll back), `majority` reads only data replicated to a majority (safe but slightly stale), `snapshot` reads from a transaction-consistent snapshot, `linearizable` reads after ack from majority (strongest, slowest). **Read preference** governs *which node* to read from — `primary` (default, always consistent), `primaryPreferred` (fail over to secondaries if primary down), `secondary` (offload reads, eventually consistent), `secondaryPreferred`, `nearest` (lowest latency, may be stale). The common pitfall: `readPreference=secondary` + `readConcern=local` gives you stale reads (a secondary may lag seconds behind primary), which breaks apps that write-then-read-immediately. The safe combo for critical reads: `readPreference=primary` + `readConcern=majority`. The fast combo for analytics: `readPreference=secondaryPreferred` + `readConcern=local` (accept staleness for throughput).
**Visual:**
```
                  What it controls          When to use
Write concern     write durability          every write
  w:0             fire-and-forget           never in prod (silent loss)
  w:1             primary ack               low-value data (logs)
  w:majority      majority replicated       financial / user data

Read concern      read freshness            critical reads
  local           primary's latest          analytics (may roll back)
  majority        committed-majority        write-then-read sequences
  snapshot        txn-consistent            transactions

Read preference   which node serves read    scaling reads
  primary         always primary (default)  strong consistency
  secondary       offload to secondaries    analytics / reporting
  nearest         lowest latency node       geo-distributed cache

Pitfall: readPref=secondary + readConcern=local = stale reads
Safe :  readPref=primary    + readConcern=majority = strong
```

sections.title: Scenario-Based Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. You're building Adobe-style creative-asset metadata storage. Each asset (image, video, PSD, AI) has different metadata fields. Why pick MongoDB over PostgreSQL?
**Answer:** Choose MongoDB because asset metadata is **polymorphic and deeply nested**. A PSD has `layers: [{name, blend_mode, opacity, masks: [...]}]`; a video has `codec, duration, resolution, keyframes: [...]`; an AI file has `artboards, vectors, embedded_fonts`. Modeling this in PostgreSQL requires either (a) a single giant sparse table with hundreds of NULL columns, (b) dozens of subtype tables with `UNION ALL` queries, or (c) a `JSONB` column — which works but loses MongoDB's first-class document query language and native array operators. MongoDB gives you `$unwind` to flatten arrays in the pipeline, array-element query operators (`{"layers.name": "Background"}` matches any array element), and atomic updates of nested fields (`$set: {"layers.0.opacity": 0.5}`). The trade-off: you lose cross-asset transactions (before 4.0) and foreign keys. If assets rarely share a transactional context (each asset is independently edited), MongoDB wins. If you need cross-asset referential integrity (e.g., "every asset must reference a valid project_id"), use PostgreSQL with JSONB. Real-world: Adobe Experience Manager stores asset metadata in MongoDB and the binary blobs in S3 — a common "document DB + object storage" pattern.
**Visual:**
```
PSD asset document:
{ _id: "asset_42",
  type: "psd",
  title: "hero_banner.psd",
  owner: "alice",
  size_bytes: 84000000,
  layers: [
    { name: "Background", opacity: 1.0, visible: true },
    { name: "Logo",       opacity: 0.8, visible: true,
      masks: [{x:0,y:0,w:100,h:50}] }
  ],
  tags: ["marketing", "q4-launch"],
  created_at: ISODate("2024-10-01T...") }

Query: "find assets where any layer is named Logo"
  db.assets.find({ "layers.name": "Logo" })

Update: "set opacity of layer 0 to 0.5"
  db.assets.updateOne({_id:"asset_42"},
    {$set: {"layers.0.opacity": 0.5}})
```

### Q2. Uber used MongoDB early but eventually migrated parts of its dispatch system to schema-on-write stores. What goes wrong with MongoDB at scale, and how do you avoid it?
**Answer:** Uber's blog post ("Why We Switched from MongoDB to PostgreSQL") cited four pain points: **(1) Schema drift** — different teams inserted documents with subtly different shapes (`trip_id` vs `tripId` vs `id`), breaking downstream consumers silently. Without DB-enforced schema, discipline erodes. **(2) Poor join performance** — MongoDB's `$lookup` is slower than a SQL JOIN, and Uber's dispatch system needed rich joins across trips, drivers, and riders. **(3) Replica-set issues** — secondaries fell behind under write pressure, causing stale reads; failover elected a stale primary once, losing data. **(4) Operational complexity** — schema migrations in MongoDB are application-level (read-old-shape, write-new-shape), harder than SQL `ALTER TABLE`. To avoid these: **(a) Enforce an application-level schema** (Mongoose, Pydantic, JSON Schema validation — MongoDB 3.6+ supports `$jsonSchema` validators at the collection level). **(b) Model joins deliberately** — if you need many joins, MongoDB is the wrong tool. **(c) Use `w:majority` and monitor replication lag** with alerts at >10s. **(d) Plan migrations** — versioned schemas with `schemaVersion` field, backward-compatible readers, dual-write during migration. Real-world: many teams successfully run MongoDB at scale (Adobe, eBay, EA Games) by enforcing these disciplines; Uber's choice was about their specific workload (high-join, transactional), not MongoDB being inherently bad.
**Visual:**
```
Schema drift example:

  Team A inserts:  { tripId: "t1", driver: "d1" }
  Team B inserts:  { trip_id: "t2", driver: "d2" }
  Team C inserts:  { id: "t3", driver_id: "d3" }

  Downstream consumer querying db.trips.find({tripId: "t1"})
  MISSES t2 and t3 silently -> data quality bug.

Mitigation:
  db.createCollection("trips", {
    validator: { $jsonSchema: {
      required: ["trip_id", "driver_id"],
      properties: {
        trip_id:   { type: "string" },
        driver_id: { type: "string" }
      }
    }}
  })
  -> inserts with wrong shape now REJECTED at DB layer
```

### Q3. You're sharding a 4 TB `orders` collection that's growing 200 GB/month. The most common queries are by `customer_id` and by `created_at` range. What shard key do you pick?
**Answer:** Use a compound shard key `{ customer_id: 1, created_at: 1 }`. Reasoning: **(1) High cardinality** — `customer_id` has many distinct values (likely millions of customers), so the key space can be split into millions of chunks (no ceiling on shard count). **(2) Even write distribution** — new orders come from many customers in parallel, so writes spread across shards naturally (unlike a monotonic `created_at` key, which would funnel all new writes to the "latest" chunk). **(3) Query locality** — queries by `customer_id` route to a single shard (the chunk map knows which shard owns that customer's range). Queries by `customer_id` + `created_at` range also route to a single shard AND use the secondary sort within the shard's index. **(4) Time-ordered within customer** — `created_at` as the second field means each customer's orders are physically clustered by time, enabling efficient range scans (`{ customer_id: X, created_at: { $gt: ... } }`). The trade-off: queries by `created_at` alone (without `customer_id`) scatter-gather — but those are typically batch/analytics queries where 5-10 second latency is acceptable. Avoid: pure `_id` (hot shard), pure `created_at` (hot shard), pure `customer_id` (loses time-ordering). Real-world: eBay shards orders by `{ seller_id: 1, created_at: 1 }` for the same reasons.
**Visual:**
```
Shard key: { customer_id: 1, created_at: 1 }

Chunk ranges:
  Shard 1: [cust_0000 - cust_4999]
  Shard 2: [cust_5000 - cust_9999]
  Shard 3: [cust_10000 - cust_14999]
  ...

Query: db.orders.find({customer_id:"cust_7321"})
  -> routes to Shard 2 (single hop, fast)

Query: db.orders.find({customer_id:"cust_7321",
                       created_at:{$gt: ISODate("2024-01-01")}})
  -> routes to Shard 2, uses (customer_id, created_at) index
  -> range scan within shard (fast)

Query: db.orders.find({created_at:{$gt: ISODate("2024-01-01")}})
  -> no customer_id -> scatter-gather (slow, but batch only)
```

### Q4. Your MongoDB cluster shows 90% CPU on one shard while others sit at 20%. Diagnose.
**Answer:** This is a classic **hot shard** — almost always caused by shard-key choice. Steps: **(1) Identify the hot chunk**: `sh.status()` shows chunk distribution; `db.orders.getShardDistribution()` shows per-shard doc counts and sizes. The hot shard has disproportionately many docs or disproportionately many ops. **(2) Check op pattern**: `mongostat` or Atlas metrics show whether the load is reads or writes. **(3) Identify the hot shard key value**: `db.orders.aggregate([{$group:{_id:"$<shard_key>", count:{$sum:1}}}, {$sort:{count:-1}}, {$limit:10}])`. If one key value dominates (e.g., a "celebrity" customer with millions of orders), you have a **chunk hotspot**. **(4) Fix**: (a) Short-term: enable **chunk migration** manually — `sh.moveChunk("orders.orders", {customer_id:"hot_cust"}, "shard_5")`. (b) Medium-term: change the shard key — MongoDB 5.0+ supports `reshardCollection` (online, but doubles disk usage during the operation). (c) Long-term: pick a key with better distribution, often hashed: `db.collection.createIndex({customer_id:"hashed"})` then shard by `{customer_id:"hashed", created_at:1}`. **(5) Also check**: a non-sharded collection that should be sharded, a missing index causing full scans, or a poorly-written aggregation that doesn't use `$match` early. Real-world: a social network's "likes" collection hot-sharded because the shard key was `post_id` and a viral post got 50M likes in an hour — fixed by switching to `{post_id:"hashed", user_id:1}`.
**Visual:**
```
Diagnosis flow:

  Symptom: shard 1 CPU 90%, others 20%
    |
    v
  sh.status() -> Shard 1 has 80% of chunks
    |
    v
  db.orders.getShardDistribution() -> Shard 1 has 80% of docs
    |
    v
  Aggregate by shard key:
    {cust_42: 50M docs}  <- HOT KEY (viral customer)
    {cust_99: 0.1M docs}
    ...
    |
    v
  Mitigation:
    + Short: sh.moveChunk (manual migration)
    + Mid:   reshardCollection (5.0+, online)
    + Long:  hashed shard key {customer_id:"hashed"}

  Also rule out:
    - missing index (explain() shows COLLSCAN)
    - aggregation without $match (full scan)
    - non-sharded collection accidentally
```

### Q5. Your team uses `w:1` write concern and just lost data during a primary failover. How do you prevent recurrence?
**Answer:** With `w:1`, the primary acks the write as soon as it applies locally — but if the primary dies before replicating the write to a majority of secondaries, that write is **rolled back** when the primary rejoins (the rollback data goes to a `rollback` collection). To prevent this: **(1) Switch to `w:majority`** for any data you can't afford to lose — the primary will not ack until the write is replicated to a majority of the replica set, so any single-node failure preserves the write. This adds ~5-15 ms latency (the cost of one extra network round trip to a secondary). **(2) Also set `j:true`** if you want to survive a process crash (not just node failure) — this fsync's the journal before ack. **(3) Audit your application** — find every write path and confirm the write concern; the default is `w:1`, which is unsafe for production user data. Use a global default (`db.adminCommand({ setDefaultRWConcern: { defaultWriteConcern: { w: "majority" } } })` in 4.4+). **(4) Recover the rolled-back data** — check the old primary's `rollback` directory; the data is preserved as BSON files you can inspect and re-insert. **(5) For the absolute strongest durability**, use **transactions** with `readConcern=snapshot` and `writeConcern=majority` (multi-document ACID since 4.0). Trade-off: every step up the durability ladder adds latency — `w:majority + j:true` can be 2-3× slower than `w:1`, which matters for high-throughput workloads. Real-world: a payment system uses `w:majority + j:true` for the payment record (must not lose) but `w:1` for the audit log (eventually consistent is fine).
**Visual:**
```
Timeline of data loss:

  T=0  Client writes payment {id:p1, amount: $100} with w:1
  T=1  Primary acks ("ok") -> client considers success
  T=2  Primary streams oplog(p1) -> S1 (in flight, not applied yet)
  T=3  Primary crashes (power loss)
  T=4  Election: S2 becomes primary (S2 didn't have p1)
  T=5  Client reads p1 -> NOT FOUND (data lost)
  T=6  Old primary recovers, rejoins as secondary
       p1 in its oplog but NOT in new primary's -> ROLLBACK
       p1 saved to rollback/ collection for manual recovery

Fix: w:majority
  T=0  Client writes p1 with w:majority
  T=1  Primary applies p1, replicates to S1 and S2
  T=2  Primary waits for both acks (majority = 2 of 3)
  T=3  Primary acks ("ok")
  T=4  Primary crashes
  T=5  S2 becomes primary, has p1 -> no data loss
```

### Q6. You need to migrate a 2 TB MongoDB collection from one shard key to another with zero downtime. How?
**Answer:** Pre-5.0, this was a painful dump-and-reload with downtime. MongoDB 5.0+ added **`reshardCollection`**, an online operation that re-shards a collection without downtime. Steps: **(1) Pre-flight**: ensure cluster is healthy (no ongoing migrations, oplog windows are large, disk has 2× free space because the operation writes both old and new layouts during transition). **(2) Issue the command**: `sh.reshardCollection("db.orders", { new_key: 1, new_key2: 1 })`. **(3) Internally**: MongoDB creates a new sharded collection with the new key, sets up a **change stream** from the old collection to copy writes, bulk-copies existing documents to the new collection (in chunks, with the new shard key), and then atomically swaps the namespace pointer when the new collection is fully populated and caught up. **(4) Monitor**: `db.orders.getShardDistribution()` shows the new layout; the operation appears as `state: "ongoing"` in `config.reshardOperations`. **(5) Cutover**: when state is "completed", old chunks are dropped automatically; clients see no interruption (mongos routes to the new collection transparently). **Caveats**: takes hours to days for TB-scale (limited by disk I/O); doubles storage during operation; if aborted, rolls back cleanly. For pre-5.0 clusters: dual-write to old and new collections, backfill via mongodump/mongorestore, then atomically rename. Real-world: eBay did this for their items collection (2.5 TB) — took 36 hours, zero downtime.
**Visual:**
```
reshardCollection timeline (5.0+):

  T=0  Issue: sh.reshardCollection("orders.orders",
                                    {customer_id:1, created_at:1})
  T=1  Creates new internal collection orders.orders.reshardXXXXX
       with new shard key
  T=2  Starts change stream from old -> new (captures ongoing writes)
  T=3  Bulk-copies chunks: shard1_old -> shard1_new, shard2_old ->
       shard2_new (uses new chunk ranges)
       ... takes hours for TB-scale ...
  T=4  Catches up change stream (new collection now reflects all writes)
  T=5  Atomic namespace swap: "orders.orders" -> new collection
  T=6  Drops old collection, frees space
  T=7  state: "completed" in config.reshardOperations

  Client perspective: no downtime, mongos transparently routes
  Storage during op: ~2x (old + new exist simultaneously)
  Rollback: clean (abort drops new collection, old unchanged)
```

### Q7. You're choosing between MongoDB Atlas (managed) and self-hosted MongoDB for a Series B startup. What factors decide?
**Answer:** The decision hinges on team size, ops maturity, and scaling trajectory. **Choose Atlas if**: (1) Your team is small (<50 engineers) and you'd rather spend engineering time on product features than DB ops. (2) You need multi-region deployments fast — Atlas makes cross-region replica sets and sharded clusters a click. (3) You want automated backups, point-in-time recovery, and security audits (Atlas handles these; self-hosted requires custom tooling). (4) You value the integrated tooling (Charts, Search, App Services, Atlas Vector Search for AI). Atlas costs ~3-5× the raw EC2 cost, but the labor savings usually justify it. **Choose self-hosted if**: (1) You have strict data-residency or compliance needs requiring on-prem hardware (air-gapped environments, government work). (2) You're at extreme scale (terabytes/month growth) where the Atlas markup exceeds the cost of a dedicated DBA team — Percona and MongoDB Enterprise support cost less at scale. (3) You need exotic configurations Atlas doesn't allow (custom storage engines, specific extension versions, kernel tuning). (4) You want to avoid vendor lock-in — though MongoDB's open-source nature (SSPL license since 2018) means you can always migrate. Real-world: most Series B startups use Atlas to ship fast; many migrate to self-hosted at Series D when costs cross ~$100k/month. The third option — MongoDB-on-Kubernetes via the MongoDB Community Operator — is a middle ground for teams with strong K8s skills but limited budget.
